query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy is a solid refrigeration working medium that exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack. What single intervention could increase its integrity while preserving caloric performance in these operating regimes? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, predicted integrity and caloric outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, applicable field, pressure, temperature, and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a low-level interstitial nitrogen dopant (~0.5 at.%) into the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy will improve its load-bearing integrity by enhancing ductility and crack resistance, while retaining its large caloric response under applied magnetic and pressure fields.
generation.material_initial_state: The undoped (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy exhibits a strong solid-state caloric effect near ambient conditions but suffers from poor mechanical robustness, with a tendency to crack when loaded.
generation.intervention: Incorporate approximately 0.5 atomic % interstitial nitrogen during the alloy’s synthesis.
generation.conditions: Testing under typical refrigeration operating regimes: near room temperature, under the same applied magnetic and pressure fields that trigger the caloric phase transition, and with mechanical loads representative of device operation.
generation.structural_mediator: Interstitial nitrogen atoms are expected to occupy lattice sites, modestly increasing the stacking fault energy and promoting smoother dislocation motion. This change helps alleviate stress concentrations that lead to crack initiation without interfering with the order–disorder transition responsible for the caloric effect.
generation.mechanism: The nitrogen acts as a solid solution strengthener, facilitating dislocation glide and delaying crack nucleation. This mechanical improvement is achieved without altering the intrinsic caloric transformation, thereby balancing enhanced mechanical integrity with preserved caloric performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the undoped alloy, the nitrogen-doped variant should exhibit a significantly higher fracture toughness and ductility (i.e., increased load-bearing integrity and reduced cracking) while showing caloric effect metrics (entropy change and adiabatic temperature changes under the applied fields) that remain effectively unchanged.
generation.baseline: The original (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy has excellent caloric properties but fails under mechanical load due to its brittleness and crack susceptibility.
generation.boundary: The expected improvements apply within the operational boundaries of refrigeration devices—specifically, near room temperature, under the magnetic and pressure fields used to induce the caloric response, and within mechanical loading conditions typical of these applications.
generation.uncertainty: The precise balance between enhanced mechanical integrity and minimally altered caloric performance is subject to experimental verification. Variations in processing or slight shifts in phase transition parameters may influence the final performance, requiring careful optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of samples: one group of the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy in its pristine form and another group doped with ~0.5 at.% interstitial nitrogen under identical processing conditions. Subject both sample sets to mechanical testing (tensile and fracture toughness measurements) and caloric performance evaluation (using calorimetric measurements to assess entropy change and adiabatic temperature change) under the same applied magnetic and pressure fields at near room temperature.
measurements: Fracture toughness and tensile ductility
Microscopic observation of crack initiation and propagation (e.g., SEM, TEM)
Caloric effect metrics such as entropy change and adiabatic temperature change under prescribed field and pressure conditions
Microstructural characterization to verify nitrogen incorporation and its effect on dislocation behavior
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the interstitial nitrogen–doped alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in load-bearing integrity (i.e., no measurable increase in fracture toughness or ductility) compared to the pristine alloy, or if the caloric performance (entropy and temperature change under applied fields) is significantly degraded beyond acceptable experimental uncertainty.

ABSTRACTWe investigated the effects of interstitial N and C on the stacking fault energy (SFE) of an equiatomic CoCrNi medium entropy alloy. Results of computer modeling were compared to tensile deformation and electron microscopy data. Both N and C in solid solution increase the SFE of the face-centered cubic (FCC) alloy matrix at room temperature, with the former having a more significant effect by 240% for 0.5 at % N. Total energy calculations based on density functional theory (DFT) as well as thermodynamic modeling of the Gibbs free energy with the CALPHAD (CALculation of PHAse Diagrams) method reveal a stabilizing effect of N and C interstitials on the FCC lattice with respect to the hexagonal close-packed (HCP) CoCrNi-X (X: N, C) lattice. Scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) measurements of the width of dissociated ½<110> dislocations suggest that the SFE of CoCrNi increases from 22 to 42–44 mJ·m−2 after doping the alloy with 0.5 at. % interstitial N. The higher SFE reduces the nucleation rates of twins, leading to an increase in the critical stress required to trigger deformation twinning, an effect which can be used to design load-dependent strain hardening res

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a small, controlled addition of Nb (around 1–2 at.%) to (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 will promote the formation of fine, coherent Nb-rich precipitates that reinforce grain boundaries, thereby increasing the alloy’s load‐bearing integrity while preserving its large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation.
drafts.material_initial_state: As-cast (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy characterized by a multiphase microstructure with poor load-bearing integrity and a large caloric effect under specific operating conditions.
drafts.intervention: Microalloying via a controlled addition of Nb at ~1–2 at.% during alloy processing.
drafts.conditions: Processing in an inert atmosphere with identical melting and casting conditions to the original alloy; operating regimes using the same magnetic field (e.g., up to 5 T) and pressure ranges; temperature window encompassing the caloric phase transition.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of fine, coherent Nb-rich precipitates decorating grain boundaries and dispersing uniformly in the matrix.
drafts.mechanism: Nb addition is expected to induce precipitation strengthening by forming fine, coherent precipitates that inhibit crack initiation and propagation without significantly altering the magnetostructural transitions that drive the caloric response.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Improved mechanical integrity (enhanced toughness, increased yield strength, and reduced crack tendency) while the caloric performance (magnitude of caloric effect under applied magnetic and pressure fields) remains comparable to that of the unmodified alloy.
drafts.baseline: The original (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy exhibits a large caloric effect but has poor load-bearing capacity and is prone to cracking during operation.
drafts.boundary: The improved integrity and preserved caloric performance are expected within the established operational boundaries: magnetic fields up to ~5 T, similar pressure-field conditions used in refrigeration cycles, and temperature ranges surrounding the alloy's phase transition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the alloy: one with the standard composition and one with an additional 1–2 at.% Nb. Process both under identical conditions and subject them to identical thermomechanical treatments. Characterize the microstructure using TEM to confirm the formation of fine Nb-rich precipitates in the microalloyed sample. Then test mechanical properties (fracture toughness, yield strength) and measure the caloric effect (e.g., adiabatic temperature change under applied magnetic fields and pressure) under identical conditions.
measurements: Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) for precipitate size and distribution
Fracture toughness and yield strength via mechanical testing
Caloric effect quantification (adiabatic temperature change, entropy change) under applied magnetic field (up to ~5 T) and pressure conditions
Phase transition temperatures via Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb microalloying does not result in a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., no meaningful increase in fracture toughness or yield strength) or if it causes a detrimental shift in the caloric performance (e.g., reduced magnitude of caloric effect or significant change in phase transition temperature) relative to the baseline alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a small (≈0.2 atomic %) addition of boron to (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 will enhance its load‐bearing integrity by strengthening the grain boundaries without significantly altering the caloric (field- and pressure-induced) performance.
drafts.material_initial_state: The alloy is a high-entropy (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 solid refrigeration medium with a martensitic or similar phase transformation responsible for its large caloric response but suffers from poor load-bearing integrity and crack propagation under operating conditions.
drafts.intervention: Dope the alloy with approximately 0.2 atomic % boron during melting and casting to promote boron segregation at grain boundaries.
drafts.conditions: The alloy is operated under typical refrigeration regimes – near the transformation temperature (e.g., around 300–350 K) with applied magnetic and pressure fields as used for caloric operation. Mechanical loads approaching those that normally induce cracking in the untreated alloy are applied.
drafts.structural_mediator: Boron segregation at grain boundaries is expected to enhance intergranular cohesion and refine the microstructure without interfering with the transformation mechanism underlying the caloric effect.
drafts.mechanism: Boron atoms preferentially migrate to and decorate grain boundaries, reducing intergranular embrittlement and inhibiting crack nucleation and propagation. Because the boron content is low, it is not expected to alter the bulk phase transformation that delivers the caloric response under applied fields and pressures.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Toughness and load-bearing integrity are increased (evidenced by reduced crack formation and higher fracture toughness) relative to the as-cast alloy, while the magnitude and reversibility of the caloric response under both applied-field and pressure-field conditions remain effectively unchanged (variations within an acceptable measurement uncertainty, e.g. ±5%).
drafts.baseline: Untreated (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 exhibits a strong caloric effect under field and pressure cycling but shows poor mechanical integrity with a tendency to crack under load.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies to operational conditions typical for refrigeration applications (temperature range around 300–350 K, with applied magnetic and pressure fields as used in the current caloric operation) and under mechanical load regimes that normally precipitate crack formation in the untreated alloy.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the standard (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy and one set doped with ≈0.2 atomic % boron using identical melting and casting procedures. Subject both sets to identical thermal cycles (covering the operational temperature range) and apply identical magnetic and pressure fields to induce the caloric effect. In parallel, perform mechanical tests (fracture toughness, bending, or microindentation) to assess load-bearing integrity.
measurements: Quantitative calorimetric scans comparing the magnitude and reversibility of the caloric effect in both doped and undoped samples.
Fracture toughness measurements (or other mechanical integrity tests) to quantify improvements in load-bearing performance.
Microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM with EDS) to verify boron segregation at the grain boundaries.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples exhibit a statistically significant reduction or alteration (>±5% deviation) in the caloric response compared to the untreated alloy, or if there is no measurable improvement in fracture toughness (or an unexpected deterioration), the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount of interstitial nitrogen (around 0.5 at.%) into the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy will enhance its load‐bearing integrity by promoting improved ductility and crack resistance via increased dislocation activity and a modest raise in stacking fault energy, while preserving its large caloric response under applied magnetic and pressure fields.
drafts.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 exhibits a large caloric effect near room temperature (under applied-field and pressure-field operation) but suffers from poor load‐bearing integrity and a tendency to crack.
drafts.intervention: Incorporate a controlled, low-level interstitial nitrogen doping (~0.5 at.%) directly into the alloy during synthesis.
drafts.conditions: Tests under the same applied magnetic and pressure fields at near-ambient operational temperatures; mechanical loading conditions typical for refrigeration device use.
drafts.structural_mediator: Interstitial nitrogen atoms are expected to reside in the lattice interstices, slightly increasing the stacking fault energy and facilitating dislocation motion to blunt stress concentrations and impede crack initiation and propagation.
drafts.mechanism: The nitrogen dopants act as interstitial solid solution strengtheners. By increasing the stacking fault energy modestly, they promote easier dislocation glide and smooth plastic deformation (and possibly suppress excessive twin formation), thereby enhancing ductility and toughness without significantly disturbing the order–disorder transition that underlies the large caloric response.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped alloy, the nitrogen-doped variant will exhibit higher fracture toughness and a lower propensity for crack initiation during load-bearing. Caloric performance metrics (such as the entropy and temperature changes under applied magnetic/pressure fields) are expected to remain at least as high as in the original alloy.
drafts.baseline: The unchanged (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy has excellent solid-state caloric effects but fails as a load-bearing material due to brittleness and cracking under mechanical stress.
drafts.boundary: The improved performance is expected within the operating regimes for refrigeration devices—namely, under moderate magnetic and pressure fields, near room temperature, and within the mechanical loading limits typical for these applications.

drafts.hypothesis: Incorporating a small amount (≈3–6 vol%) of well‐dispersed, inert SiC nanoparticles into the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy will improve its load‐bearing integrity by arresting crack growth while leaving the intrinsic caloric (order–disorder) transition intact.
drafts.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy that exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but suffers from poor mechanical robustness and crack propagation.
drafts.intervention: Introduce 3–6 vol% SiC nanoparticles into the melt or via powder consolidation, ensuring uniform dispersion in the matrix during processing.
drafts.conditions: Operable under the same applied-field (e.g., magnetic field if applicable or other relevant field) and pressure conditions in the temperature range used for refrigeration (near room temperature), without exceeding load conditions that could induce phase changes.
drafts.structural_mediator: The uniformly distributed SiC nanoparticles serve as crack arrestors and act as stress concentrators that promote load sharing and obstruct crack propagation.
drafts.mechanism: The SiC reinforcement enhances integrity via load transfer and impeding dislocation movement (Orowan strengthening), thus delaying crack initiation and growth without perturbing the underlying order–disorder transition that gives rise to the caloric effect.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The alloy will show significantly improved fracture toughness and tensile strength (e.g., a ≥20% improvement) while its caloric performance (entropy change and transition temperature) remains essentially unchanged compared to the unreinforced alloy.
drafts.baseline: The as-produced (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy has excellent caloric response but cracks readily under mechanical load due to poor load-bearing integrity.
drafts.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective only if the nanoparticle volume fraction is kept low (≈3–6 vol%) so that the matrix’s transformation characteristics (and hence caloric performance) are not disturbed; it applies under the operating regimes used in solid-state refrigeration where moderate fields and pressures are used.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy reinforced with 5 vol% SiC nanoparticles and one set of control samples without reinforcement. Process both sets identically. Subject the samples to uniaxial tensile testing and fracture toughness assessment, as well as caloric performance evaluation (measuring the entropy change and transition temperature under applied-field/pressure cycling).
measurements: Tensile strength
Fracture toughness or crack propagation resistance
Caloric entropy change (ΔS) during the transition
Transition temperature of the order–disorder transformation
Crack density or failure strain under mechanical load
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the reinforced alloy does not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement (e.g., ≥20% increase) in mechanical integrity (tensile strength/fracture toughness) or if its caloric performance (entropy change and transition temperature) is degraded by more than approximately 10% compared to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.
